History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
54-year-old male with untreated hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia presented via video visit with 2-hour, sudden-onset, mid-sternal pressure-type chest discomfort radiating to the left shoulder/arm with dyspnoea, light-headedness, and nausea; ambulance arranged for suspected acute coronary syndrome.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Mid-sternal chest “pressure” (“like someone sitting on my chest”).  
• Onset/duration: Sudden while digging in the garden ≈2 h ago; constant since onset.  
• Severity: 7/10 at onset and presently.  
• Radiation: To left shoulder and arm; no radiation to back, head, or right arm.  
• Associated symptoms: Shortness of breath, light-headedness, persistent nausea (no vomiting), recent months of exertional dyspnoea with stair/ uphill walking, calf pain, and leg swelling.  
• Exacerbating/relieving factors: Began with mild exertion; unchanged with rest; no treatments attempted.  
• Pertinent negatives: No dysphagia, no urinary or bowel changes, no pain radiating to back, no vomiting.

Past Medical History:
• Hypertension – untreated.  
• Hypercholesterolaemia – untreated.  
No other chronic illnesses reported.

Medications:
• No regular medications.  
• “Don’t take any of those medications” (none specified).  
Allergies: Not documented.

Social History:
• Lives with wife at home; independent in ADLs though limits activity due to breathlessness.  
• Smoker (quantity/frequency not documented).  
• Alcohol and other substance use: not discussed.  
• Occupation/activities: Gardening fortnightly.

Family History:
• Not discussed.

Physical Examination:
Vitals: Not recorded (remote consult).  
General, cardiovascular, respiratory, abdominal, neuro: Not recorded.

Investigations:
• None performed yet.  
• Ambulance called for urgent hospital assessment (anticipate ECG, cardiac biomarkers, imaging).

Assessment & Plan:

Overall Impression:
Acute coronary syndrome (ACS) is highly suspected given typical chest pressure with left-arm radiation and multiple cardiovascular risk factors; pulmonary embolism remains a significant alternate consideration.

DDx Integration (brief):
1. Acute coronary syndrome – supports: typical pressure, left-arm radiation, nausea, dyspnoea, untreated HTN/cholesterol, smoker.  
2. Pulmonary embolism – supports: acute dyspnoea, calf pain & leg swelling; opposes: non-pleuritic pain, no hemoptysis.  
3. Aortic dissection – supports: abrupt onset, HTN; opposes: pain not tearing, no back radiation.

Issue 1: Suspected Acute Coronary Syndrome  
Assessment: High clinical suspicion based on symptom quality/radiation and risk profile.  
Plan:  
• 999 ambulance activated; advise patient to remain calm, sit upright, take sips of water.  
• Paramedics to obtain vitals, 12-lead ECG, ASA, nitrates, oxygen as indicated.  
• ED / cardiology evaluation with serial ECGs, troponins, CXR, and further management per ACS protocol.  
• Clinician to provide handover to paramedics and await consultant update.  
• Safety-net: patient advised to call back if worsening symptoms while waiting.

Issue 2: Possible Pulmonary Embolism / Venous Thrombo-embolism  
Assessment: Calf pain & leg swelling with acute chest symptoms raise PE concern.  
Plan:  
• Flag to receiving team; consider D-dimer, CT pulmonary angiography if ACS excluded.  
• Duplex US of lower extremities if indicated.

Issue 3: Cardiovascular Risk Factor Management  
Assessment: Long-standing untreated hypertension and hypercholesterolaemia, ongoing smoking.  
Plan (post-acute episode):  
• Arrange follow-up primary care appointment to initiate guideline-based antihypertensive and statin therapy.  
• Smoking cessation counselling; offer pharmacotherapy/referral to cessation services.  
• Lifestyle counselling (diet, exercise) once cleared by cardiology.

General plan items:  
• Follow-up tele-visit after hospital discharge to review diagnoses, medications, and risk factor control.  
• Document allergies and full medication list at next contact.

Quality checks:
● Missing elements: Allergies, complete medication reconciliation, family history, vitals, physical exam findings – not obtainable in remote emergency context.  
● No contradictions identified between transcript and DDx.  
● Transcript quality adequate; brief miscommunication noted when patient answered smoking status instead of pain status, but clarified later.
